verdicts.reason: One asks whether boundary/degenerate/equality cases the argument itself exposes are treated, the other asks whether each variable's logical binding stays unambiguous.
One is about variable binding staying unambiguous, the other about arithmetic/computational steps agreeing with their own inputs.

One asks whether a general claim is proved for an arbitrary member rather than sampled instances, the other asks whether an abstract construction is anchored by a worked instance; a post can do one without the other.
One is a general test that every assertion in the chain has support, the other is narrowly about whether a named result's specific preconditions are verified when applied.
One asks whether the argument confronts its own obvious weak point, the other asks whether stated confidence/hedging matches the support actually given.
One asks whether prose (not just formula arrangement) carries the reasoning, the other asks whether a spatial/relational configuration is reconstructible from words alone.
One is about variables' logical status staying fixed, the other about whether stated claims/lemmas are actually proved and clearly paired to their proofs.
One tests that every assertion has visible support, the other tests that displayed computations are internally consistent with their inputs.
One is about dismissive language not landing on the crux, the other about delegated/omitted work being specified precisely enough to reproduce.
One checks that an applied result's own preconditions are verified, the other checks whether the post's own method is stated in a reusable, condition-bearing way.

One is about whether compressed steps leave enough handholds to be rebuilt, the other about whether effort is allocated to the hard step rather than routine ones; a compressed-but-reconstructible step can still be under-cared-for if it is the crux.
One tests visible support for each assertion, the other tests whether stated confidence/hedging matches the support actually present.

One is about HOW a general claim is established (argued for an arbitrary member vs. sampled), the other about WHETHER any stated claim is discharged at all; a claim can be discharged yet discharged by sampling.
One is about a named result's preconditions being verified, the other about boundary/degenerate/equality cases exposed by the argument's own steps being addressed.

One asks whether the core reason the argument works can be stated in one sentence, the other asks whether a standard argument-shape (induction, contradiction, etc.) has all its required components present.
One is about a named result's conditions being verified, the other about displayed computations holding together internally.

One asks whether the mechanism that makes the argument work is extractable in one sentence after reading, the other asks whether the post itself states a motivation for why the decisive move was tried; a clear mechanism can be foregrounded with no stated motivation, or vice versa.
One is about whether invoked tools' power matches what each step needs, the other about whether case-work avoids redundant repetition.
One asks whether introduced auxiliary objects are used and their purpose legible, the other asks whether variables' logical binding/quantification status stays unambiguous.

One asks whether the stated value is actually derived by the shown reasoning, the other asks whether the post subsequently checks/verifies that value; a value can be derived but never checked, or checked without being properly derived.
One tests exhaustive coverage of a case split, the other tests whether the listed cases avoid redundant repeated work.
One is about the overall argument's decisive reason being extractable, the other specifically about whether a chosen frame/coordinate system is justified.

One assumes an answer exists and asks whether it is actually derived by the reasoning shown, the other is a more basic gate on whether the post makes any substantive attempt at all rather than a bare answer or remark.

One requires the crux to be explicitly named in a sentence, the other only requires effort/care to be visibly concentrated on the hard step; X's own rubric treats effort-only allocation as merely partial credit, distinguishing it from Y's full criterion.
One is a substantive judgment about whether the key obstacle is named, the other is a purely mechanical count of display-math blocks with no bearing on that judgment.
One is about boundary/degenerate/equality cases being treated, the other about displayed computations agreeing with their own inputs.
One is about an explicit problem-to-problem reduction being announced and justified, the other about ongoing faithfulness to the problem's stated constraints and defined terms throughout.
One is a substantive judgment about whether a cited theorem's hypotheses are verified, the other is a purely mechanical word count with no bearing on that judgment.

One is about every symbol (especially self-coined ones) being defined before its first use, the other about statement-supplied symbols keeping one stable meaning and not being rebound; a symbol can be promptly defined yet later reused for two things, or vice versa.
One is a basic gate on whether the post makes a real attempt at all rather than a question or bare answer, the other asks whether it says something that generalizes beyond the specific problem.
One is about delegated/omitted work being specified precisely, the other about cases being organized to avoid repetition.
One asks whether the crux is explicitly named, the other asks whether every distinctive hypothesis actually does work in the argument (tested by mentally deleting each one).
One is about whether stated claims/lemmas are proved, the other about whether the technique itself is made reusable/portable beyond this problem.
One is about the argument's decisive reason being extractable in one sentence, the other about a spatial/relational configuration being reconstructible from the words alone.
One asks whether the crux is explicitly identified, the other asks whether dismissive language avoids landing on it; a post can name the crux and still wave it away, or vice versa.
One is about a single line of attack persisting to a stated conclusion, the other about displayed computations holding together internally.

One tests that every assertion in the chain has support, the other specifically that explicitly stated claims/lemmas are discharged with clear boundaries; a post can support all its small steps without ever flagging a formal claim, or discharge a stated claim while an unrelated assertion elsewhere lacks support.

One requires the route to be stated before technical work begins, the other requires the decisive move specifically to carry a stated reason; a generic upfront plan can lack any motivation for the key move, or motivation can appear midway with no upfront plan.
One is about the decisive move carrying a stated reason, the other about the argument's obvious weak point being addressed.
One is about a named result's own preconditions being verified, the other about stated claims/lemmas being discharged.
One is about dismissive language not landing on the crux, the other about borrowed external results being specifically identified.
One is about a named result's preconditions being verified, the other about the post offering a claim that survives beyond the problem's particulars.

One asks whether the technique itself is stated as reusable with a transferable condition, the other asks whether the post makes any true statement that generalizes beyond the problem's specifics; a portable method can be stated with no further generalizing remark about the result, or vice versa.
One is about faithfulness to the problem's stated conditions and defined terms, the other about self-coined symbols being defined before use.
One is about the final claim covering everything the question demands, the other specifically about symmetry/scaling-type reductions being licensed and scaling undone.
One is about the decisive move carrying a stated reason, the other about dismissive language not landing on the crux.
One is about the final claim covering every part of what was asked, the other about faithfulness to the problem's own stated conditions and terms.
One is about the argument's decisive reason being extractable in one sentence, the other about dismissive language not landing on the crux.
One is about exhaustive coverage of a stated case division, the other about boundary/degenerate/equality values the argument exposes being addressed even absent any case division.
One is about the decisive reason being extractable in one sentence, the other about the method being stated as portable/reusable with its own condition.
One tests visible support for every assertion, the other tests treatment of boundary/degenerate/equality cases the argument exposes.
Both ask only whether the post states its intended method or line of attack before the technical/computational work begins.
One is about cases being organized without redundant repetition, the other about non-mathematical text not displacing the argument.

One asks whether a single line of attack persists to a conclusion, the other asks whether abandoned attempts are pruned or clearly marked as exploration; a switched line can still be clearly marked, or a persistent line can still have unmarked clutter around it.

One is narrowly about a chosen frame (coordinates, parametrization, etc.) being justified, the other about the decisive/non-obvious move in general carrying a reason, which need not be a frame choice at all.
One is about non-mathematical material not displacing the argument, the other about the post being intelligible without reading the surrounding thread discussion.
One is about invoked tool strength matching what each step needs, the other about non-mathematical text not displacing the argument.
One is about delegated/omitted work being specified precisely, the other about borrowed external results being specifically identified.
One assumes a conclusion exists and checks it covers everything asked, the other is a more basic gate on whether the post is a substantive attempt at all rather than a question or bare answer.
One is about boundary/degenerate/equality cases being treated, the other about stated claims/lemmas being discharged.

One is broader, testing faithfulness to stated conditions/constraints/defined terms generally, the other narrower, testing only that statement-supplied symbols/notation are not rebound; a constraint can be dropped with no notation clash, or notation can stay stable while a defined term's meaning drifts.
One is about a named result's preconditions being verified, the other about variables' logical binding staying unambiguous.
One is about the decisive move carrying a stated reason, the other about the post asserting something that generalizes beyond the specific problem.
One is about an explicit problem reduction being announced and justified, the other about the final claim covering everything the question demands.

One is about a variable's logical status (arbitrary, fixed, quantified) staying consistent, the other about symbols being defined before their first use; a symbol can be defined promptly yet its status still shift later, or vice versa.

One asks whether the mechanism that makes the argument work is extractable in a sentence, the other asks whether the problem's difficulty/trap is explicitly named; a post can clearly foreground its working mechanism without ever labeling what was hard, or vice versa.
One is about displayed computations holding together internally, the other about stated claims/lemmas being discharged.
One tests visible support for every assertion, the other tests that variables keep a definite logical status.

One is about a cited external result's own preconditions being satisfied, the other about faithfulness to the conditions given in the problem statement itself; these are conditions from different sources.
Both ask only whether every symbol/letter is defined or declared before it first appears in the text.
One requires a route to be stated before the technical work begins in general, the other specifically requires a chosen frame/coordinate system to carry a reason for that particular choice.

One is a general test that any problem-to-problem reduction is announced and justified, the other is a narrower subtype specifically about symmetry/scaling/relabelling reductions with the extra requirement that any scaling be undone in the final answer; a non-symmetry reduction only engages X, and a scaling reduction that forgets to undo scaling fails Y while still satisfying X.
